tasks.locator: Executive Summary › Brief Description of Issues for Discussion at the AC, 1st paragraph (pp. 8-9); Efficacy Issue #1, 9th paragraph (p. 36)
tasks.extracted: The reviewers take it as a reasonable assumption that functional unblinding and expectation bias influenced the observed treatment effects to some degree, a contribution they cannot quantify; in summary, the two trials appear to show clinically meaningful effects whose interpretation is challenging because of likely unblinding and expectation bias.

tasks.locator: 3.1.2.1.1 Study Design, 3rd paragraph; Approach to Psychotherapy, 4th paragraph (pp. 17-18); Efficacy Issue #3, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (pp. 38-39)
tasks.extracted: No study had an arm without the psychological intervention or with the intervention alone; the integrative sessions were not standardized and were left mainly to the individual therapist; the necessity of psychotherapy was assumed, so whether it contributes to the effect is unknown.

tasks.locator: 3.2.2.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 29-30); Table 8 and 3.2.2.3, 2nd paragraph (p. 32)
tasks.extracted: The only outcome reported after week 18 is a single observational visit (MPLONG), attended by 56 of MAPP1's and 81 of MAPP2's participants a median 23.4 and 8.5 months after the last treatment; the FDA judges MPLONG not properly designed to evaluate durability.

tasks.locator: Question 5, Vote Result and Committee Discussion
tasks.extracted: The FDA's advisory committee voted 9 to 2 that the available data did not show effectiveness, many members citing functional unblinding, the lack of management of expectation bias and selection bias; the two yes voters weighed the large effect sizes.

tasks.locator: 11.3 Additional Phase 3 Results (p. 130); 11.3.1, Table 30 and Worst-Case Sensitivity Analysis (p. 131); 11.3.2 and Table 31 (pp. 131-132)

MAPP2 de facto (52 vs 44) difference −8.93 (−13.69 to −4.17), P = 0.0003; no worst-case result is given for MAPP2.

tasks.locator: Executive Summary › Brief Description of Issues for Discussion at the AC, 1st paragraph

tasks.locator: 3.2.3 Efficacy Issues in Detail › Efficacy Issue #1, 3rd and 7th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Participants on MDMA guessed with more certainty (I think 15.4%, I am positive 78.8%) than those on placebo (31.8% and 43.2%), which the FDA reads as suggesting the bias may be imbalanced between arms; since 94% of the MDMA arm knew or thought they had the drug, expectation bias could have acted more on that arm; its contribution remains difficult to quantify.

tasks.locator: Pertinent Drug Development and Regulatory History › Highlights of Regulatory History, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: At the 2016 end-of-phase-2 meeting the FDA questioned the adequacy of the blind and suggested niacin or low-dose MDMA as comparators with enough physiological effect to mask placebo; the sponsor preferred inert placebo and the two did not agree; the 2017 special protocol assessment letter accepted inactive placebo while stating continued concern about the adequacy of the blind.

tasks.locator: Efficacy Issue #1, 4th paragraph

tasks.locator: p. 1687, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; p. 1688, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Second Matters Arising on MAPP1: the inert placebo was insufficient for blinding; from the trial's figures 81 of 90 participants (90%) may have guessed their treatment correctly; with participants likely to know their allocation, the MDMA arm gains placebo effects and the placebo arm may suffer nocebo effects; trialists should at least be required to collect data on blinding, which the 2010 CONSORT update stopped requiring; the letter adds no data. tasks.locator: Questions to the Committee, question 1, Committee Discussion
tasks.extracted: Members said functional unblinding and expectation bias may have played a role in the efficacy results and some said these biases alone could account for the short-term results; on durability, many said there were too many confounders to tease apart in the small data set; members suggested a two-by-two factorial design for the psychological intervention, and some were concerned that therapist unblinding and the therapists' power of suggestion could have influenced the results.

tasks.locator: Questions to the Committee, question 2, Committee Discussion

The minutes do not mention the MP4 site or the misconduct behind the retractions.

tasks.locator: Questions to the Committee, question 4, Committee Discussion
tasks.extracted: Many members said the risk of harm during impairment was not fully characterized and suggested two licensed therapists, training by an independent outside group rather than the sponsor, medical staff on site, safety reporting mechanisms outside the treatment centres, and more complete ECG, laboratory and vital-sign data.

tasks.locator: Disclaimer statement
tasks.extracted: The briefing package was prepared by the FDA for the committee; its conclusions are those of individual reviewers, not the final position of the reviewers, the division or the office, and it may not include every issue relevant to the final decision, which awaits the committee's input and the completed reviews.

tasks.locator: Executive Summary › Brief Description of Issues for Discussion at the AC, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: The reviewers write that the studies are nearly impossible to blind: about 90% of those given MDMA and 75% of those given placebo guessed their assignment in a post-study survey, the in-session monitors could probably tell assignment from behaviour, and it is reasonable to assume that functional unblinding and expectation bias affected the treatment effects to some extent.

tasks.locator: Executive Summary, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 9); 3.2.2.1 Populations and Baseline Characteristics for MPLONG, 1st paragraph (p. 29)
tasks.extracted: The follow-up visit, 6 months to more than 2 years after treatment, lost about 25% of participants, had variable timing and was confounded by interim treatments; the FDA judges it not properly designed to evaluate durability. The contribution of psychotherapy was never characterized: every arm of every study included it.

tasks.locator: Executive Summary, 4th to 6th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Cardiac safety is not well characterized and the QT assessment is incomplete; liver tests were not done in phase 3; the studies did not capture effects deemed positive, favourable or neutral, such as euphoria, although the FDA had advised collecting abuse-related adverse events, which limits the abuse-potential assessment.

tasks.locator: Midomafetamine Effects Perceived as Positive Were Not Recorded, 1st paragraph (p. 50); 3.3.4.2.2, paragraphs after the quoted 2017 advice (p. 56)
tasks.extracted: Despite the FDA's advice of 9 March 2017 that abuse-related adverse events be documented in all phase 1, 2 and 3 studies, the application states that effects judged neutral, positive or favourable were not systematically collected as adverse events; the FDA says this was not consistent with its 2017 advice and excluded most of the events used in an abuse-potential evaluation.

tasks.locator: Sources of Data for Efficacy; Table 1 (pp. 15-16); 3.3.1 Sources of Data for Safety (p. 39); Tables 10 and 11 (p. 40)
tasks.extracted: Efficacy rests on MAPP1 and MAPP2, with the open-label MP16 and MAPPUSX not meant to provide substantial evidence, and the follow-up MPLONG; the safety database covers 426 people exposed in the sponsor's trials and 50 in NIDA studies, and the serious-event tables list phase 2 studies (MP-1, MP-2, MP-8, MP-12, MT-1, MDA-1). tasks.locator: 7.7.1.1 Summary (Neuropsychological and Physiological Effects), 1st paragraph (p. 86); Table 29, MP-4 row (p. 124)

tasks.locator: Table 7, UFEC row (p. 50); 6.8, 4th paragraph (p. 68); Table 32 and its footnotes (p. 135)
tasks.extracted: The sponsor's briefing document lists a self-reported, sponsor-developed measure of health-care use (UFEC) among the phase 3 trials' exploratory measures but gives no result for it, and it is absent from the summary of exploratory results (Table 32); the follow-up study MPLONG collected health-economics data, which the document does not report; Table 32 classes the quality-of-life measure EQ-5D-5L as suggestive of a treatment effect in both studies although its nominal P values were 0.0394 (MAPP1) and 0.0557 (MAPP2).

tasks.locator: Questions 5 and 6, Vote Results and Committee Discussion
tasks.extracted: Advisory committee votes: effectiveness, yes 2, no 9, abstain 0, many members citing functional unblinding, the lack of management of expectation bias and selection bias, the yes voters weighing the large effect sizes; benefits with the FDA's proposed REMS outweighing risks, yes 1, no 10, abstain 0, many members saying more efficacy and safety data were needed.

tasks.locator: Executive Summary › Brief Description of Issues for Discussion at the AC, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The reviewers judge the studies nearly impossible to blind, with participants and probably the in-session monitors aware of allocation, and both biases likely to have influenced the effects to an unquantifiable degree; the follow-up lost about 25% and was confounded by interim treatments; the contribution of psychotherapy was never characterized.

tasks.locator: 3.2.2.1, 1st paragraph (p. 29); Table 8 (p. 32); Benefit-Risk Framework, Benefits row, 5th bullet (p. 66)
tasks.extracted: At a single observational visit 6 months to more than 2 years after treatment, among those who attended, the difference from placebo was maintained (-14.7 in MAPP1 and -11.96 in MAPP2), but the FDA judges the follow-up not properly designed to evaluate durability.

tasks.locator: Midomafetamine Effects Perceived as Positive Were Not Recorded, 1st paragraph (p. 50); 3.3.4.2.2, paragraphs after the quoted 2017 advice (p. 56)
tasks.extracted: Positive, favourable or neutral drug effects were not systematically collected as adverse events, which the FDA says was not consistent with its 2017 advice and excluded most of the events used in an abuse-potential evaluation.

tasks.locator: Efficacy Issue #3: Contribution of Psychotherapy to Efficacy, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: There are no data on MDMA without psychotherapy or on the psychotherapy against no treatment; the manual leaves therapists considerable flexibility; the difference between arms suggests MDMA adds an effect but says nothing about the psychotherapy's own contribution.

tasks.locator: Efficacy Issue #1, 8th and 9th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The FDA weighs both sides: the persisting difference might suggest a true drug effect, but how long expectation bias lasts is unknown and the follow-up has major limitations; two positive trials appear to show clinically meaningful effects whose interpretation is challenging because of likely unblinding and expectation bias.

tasks.locator: 6.8 MPLONG Study Design, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 67-68); 6.8.1 (p. 68); Table 29, MAPPUSX row (p. 121), and its footnote d (p. 127)
tasks.extracted: MPLONG was observational and voluntary (participants were strongly encouraged to join, at least 6 months after their last session): MAPP1's participants enrolled after its database lock and unblinding, MAPP2's stayed blinded until its database lock and their MPLONG visit; interim psychotherapy, medicines and illicit MDMA use were collected but are not reported in the document; 32 MAPP1 placebo participants received open-label MDMA in the extension study MAPPUSX, from March 2021 (whether before or after their follow-up visit is not stated); the results come from an interim study report.

tasks.locator: p. 1687, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; p. 1688, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Second Matters Arising on MAPP1: the inert placebo was insufficient for blinding; from the trial's figures 81 of 90 participants (90%) may have guessed their treatment correctly; with participants likely to know their allocation, the MDMA arm gains placebo effects and the placebo arm may suffer nocebo effects; trialists should at least be required to collect data on blinding, which the 2010 CONSORT update stopped requiring; the letter adds no data. Editors' note: the trial reports at least 9 wrong beliefs, so 81 is the most who could have guessed right.

tasks.locator: Supplementary Table S3, last row (PDFs/MDMA/Mitchell_2023_MAPP2_Supplement.pdf)
tasks.extracted: Of the 8 placebo participants with missing data, one chose to discontinue treatment because they believed they were receiving placebo (missing the assessment after the second session); the others chose to stop, declined to participate, withdrew consent, were lost to follow-up or had adverse events (passive suicidal ideation; abdominal pain).

tasks.locator: 7.7.1.1 Summary, 2nd paragraph (p. 86); 7.7.3.1, 5th paragraph (p. 97); 7.7.4.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 98); 7.7.5, 2nd paragraph, and 7.7.7, 1st paragraph (p. 99)
tasks.extracted: By the sponsor's account, the phase 3 programme collected the subjective effects of MDMA (sensation, perception, mood, cognition) only when reported as adverse events and made no direct assessment of the subjective effects bearing on nonmedical use, and the development programme did not collect desired (positive) effects as abuse-related events; abuse-related events of special interest, pre-agreed with the FDA, were none; no ECGs were taken after dosing in phase 2 or phase 3, no laboratory tests after dosing in phase 3, and most of the sponsor's trials captured no laboratory data bearing on liver injury.

tasks.locator: 7.7.1.1 Summary (Neuropsychological and Physiological Effects), 1st paragraph (p. 86); Table 29, MP-4 row (p. 124)
tasks.extracted: Under the risk of serious harm from impairment during MDMA's altered mental state, the sponsor states that one participant in the phase 2 study MP-4 sustained serious harm resulting from significant breaches of boundaries, unethical conduct and sexual misconduct; the event was reported to the sponsor after the study had concluded and was investigated, with no evidence of misconduct with other participants at the site. In the table of studies (p. 124), MP-4 is a single-site study in Canada (October 2014 to October 2016) with 6 participants in its first stage (2 placebo, 4 MDMA).

tasks.locator: Supplementary Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (PDFs/MDMA/Mitchell_2023_MAPP2_Supplement.pdf)
tasks.extracted: Tipping-point analysis assuming missing CAPS-5 values missing not at random (50 imputed datasets combined by Rubin's rules): with only one MDMA participant missing the final (visit 19) value there was no tipping point from penalizing the MDMA arm, and the result stayed significant until the missing placebo values were shifted 28 points toward improvement (still significant at 27); a worst-case analysis is said to have been done, but no result is given.
